# Concepts

## Anycast Gateway (anycast ip gateway, distributed gateway)

A lighter alternative to DvR. Several BEBs of the same L2 VSN share one gateway IP and MAC (configured the same on each), without controllers or leaves. Each BEB answers ARP for the gateway and routes locally.

See: `ip anycast-gateway <gateway-ip> [vrid <1-255>] / ip anycast-gateway enable`, `l2 ping anycast-gw <isid> [vrf <vrf>]`

## Auto-sense (autosense, zero touch port, port states, uni state, nni state)

Auto-sense ports configure themselves based on what is connected. They start in WAIT and listen for LLDP. A fabric switch makes the port an NNI, an FA AP/proxy makes it FA, an IP phone makes it VOICE, and without LLDP the port becomes a UNI with NAC (EAP/NEAP) and onboarding/data I-SIDs. The dynamic config does not show in the running-config; check the state with `show interfaces gigabitEthernet auto-sense`.

See: `show interfaces gigabitEthernet auto-sense [<ports>]`, `auto-sense enable`, `auto-sense onboarding i-sid <isid>`, `auto-sense no-nni`

## B-VLAN / B-VID (backbone vlan, bvlan, primary b-vlan, ect)

The backbone VLANs that carry fabric traffic between nodes, usually two (e.g. 4051 and 4052). Each B-VLAN uses its own equal-cost tree algorithm, so traffic is spread over different paths. The B-VLAN IDs and the primary B-VLAN must be the same on every node, otherwise no adjacency forms. B-VLANs have no ports as members; they run over the NNIs.

See: `spbm 1 b-vid <bvid1>-<bvid2> primary <bvid1>`, `show isis spbm unicast-fib [b-mac <bmac>] [vlan <bvid>] [summary]`

## BEB / BCB (backbone edge bridge, backbone core bridge)

A BEB is a fabric node where services start or end, because it has I-SIDs, UNIs or VRFs. A BCB only forwards fabric traffic (MAC-in-MAC) and knows nothing about the services. One switch can be both. Nodes with the IS-IS overload bit set are not used as transit (BCB) paths.

See: `show isis spbm nick-name [home | remote]`, `overload`

## CFM (connectivity fault management, 802.1ag, mep, mip, l2 ping, l2 traceroute)

Ethernet OAM (802.1ag), the basis for l2 ping, l2 traceroute and l2 tracetree in the fabric. Each switch has a MEP on the B-VLANs. Nodes without CFM do not answer, so they are missing from traces.

See: `cfm spbm enable`, `l2 ping vlan <bvid> routernodename <isis-hostname>`, `l2 traceroute vlan <bvid> routernodename <isis-hostname>`

## CLIP (circuitless ip, loopback)

A circuitless IP is a loopback interface that is always up. It is used as a stable management address, as the router ID and as the IP shortcut source address.

See: `show ip interface [vrf <vrf>]`

## CoA (change of authorization, dynamic authorization, radius disconnect, rfc 5176)

Change of Authorization lets the RADIUS server (ExtremeControl) act on an existing session, e.g. re-authenticate a client or disconnect it after a policy change. On the switch you configure the NAC as a dynamic-server client and enable it on the ports.

See: `radius dynamic-server client <nac-ip> secret <secret> enable`

## DvR (distributed virtual routing, dvr controller, dvr leaf, dvr domain)

Distributed Virtual Routing puts the same gateway IP on every switch in a DvR domain, so traffic is routed at the first hop. Controllers own the config (subnets, gateway IP) and push it to the leaves. Host routes (/32) of clients are shared in the fabric, which avoids hairpinning through a central router. A leaf needs the dvr-leaf-mode boot flag, which wipes non-DvR L3 config.

See: `show dvr`, `show dvr members [controller | leaf]`, `show dvr host-entries [ipv4 <ip> | l2isid <isid> | vrf <vrf>]`, `dvr gw-ipv4 <gateway-ip> / dvr enable`

## EAP / NEAP (802.1x, eapol, mac authentication, mab, nac, mhmv, mhsa)

EAP (802.1X) authenticates clients that have a supplicant. NEAP authenticates clients without one by their MAC address via RADIUS (like MAB on Cisco). With MHMV (multiple hosts, multiple VLANs), every client on a port authenticates on its own and ExtremeControl can assign it a VLAN/I-SID. Since 9.3, NEAP fallback tries NEAP when EAP fails. Global `eapol enable` is required.

See: `show eapol sessions {eap | neap} [verbose] [<ports>]`, `eapol status auto`, `eapol multihost eap-oper-mode {mhmv | mhsa}`

## Fabric Attach (fa, fa proxy, fa client, fa server)

An LLDP extension that lets non-fabric devices (APs, EXOS/ERS switches as FA proxies, cameras) ask the fabric switch (the FA server) for I-SID-to-VLAN assignments. The edge device then only tags the VLAN, and the fabric switch maps it to the I-SID. With authentication, assignments can be secured with a key.

See: `show fa elements [<ports>]`, `show fa assignment [<ports>]`, `auto-sense fa wap-type1 i-sid <isid>`

## Guest and fail-open I-SID (guest isid, fail-open isid, critical vlan, radius down)

A guest I-SID is for clients that fail or skip authentication. A fail-open I-SID is used for new clients when all RADIUS servers are unreachable, so the network keeps working in a degraded mode. Fail-open needs RADIUS reachability checks to detect the outage.

See: `eapol port <ports> guest-isid <isid>`, `eapol port <ports> fail-open-isid <isid>`, `radius reachability mode {status-server | use-radius}`

## I-SID (service instance identifier, isid, service id)

The 24-bit service ID in the fabric, comparable to a VLAN ID or VNI in the backbone. An L2 VSN, an L3 VSN (VRF), the vIST and DvR domains each use their own I-SID. Only the I-SID has to match across the fabric; the local VLAN ID mapped to it can differ per switch. Values above 15999999 are reserved by the system (onboarding uses 15999999 by default).

See: `show i-sid [<isid>]`, `vlan i-sid <vid> <isid>`, `show isis spbm i-sid {all | config | discover} [id <isid>] [vlan <bvid>]`

## IP Shortcuts (grt shortcuts, global routing table over spb)

Routing in the Global Routing Table (GRT) over the fabric. IS-IS advertises the GRT prefixes and forwards them directly from BEB to BEB, without transit VLANs or a separate IGP. The source address for locally generated traffic is a CLIP (`ip-source-address`).

See: `spbm 1 ip enable`, `redistribute direct [route-map <map>] / isis apply redistribute direct`

## Junos commit model (candidate config, commit, rollback, commit confirmed)

Changes go into a candidate config and only take effect with `commit`. `show | compare` shows the diff, `commit confirmed <min>` rolls back on its own unless you confirm, and `rollback <n>` loads one of the last 50 committed configs. The VOSS equivalent of the safety net is `reset -in` before the change.

See: `show | compare / commit check / commit confirmed <minutes>`, `reset -in <[d:][hh:]mm>`

## L2 VSN (layer 2 virtual service network, l2vsn, stretched vlan)

A Layer 2 service across the fabric: all BEBs that map a VLAN (or S-UNI/T-UNI endpoints) to the same I-SID form one broadcast domain. BUM traffic only goes to the BEBs that have the I-SID. MACs are learned as "client MAC behind remote B-MAC".

See: `vlan i-sid <vid> <isid>`, `show vlan remote-mac-table <vid>`, `l2 tracetree <bvid> <isid> [routernodename <name>]`

## L3 VSN (layer 3 virtual service network, ip vpn, ipvpn, vrf over spb)

A VRF stretched over the fabric. Each BEB binds the VRF to the same L3 VSN I-SID (ipvpn), and IS-IS carries the VRF's routes between them, so no BGP/MPLS is needed. Routes are only advertised after you redistribute them (`isis redistribute direct`) and apply the change (`isis apply redistribute`). Inter-VRF leaking uses IS-IS accept policies.

See: `router vrf <vrf>`, `show ip ipvpn [vrf <vrf>]`, `isis accept i-sid <isid> enable`, `isis apply redistribute <protocol> vrf <vrf>`

## MACsec (802.1ae, mka, cak, ckn, sak, connectivity association)

Hop-by-hop encryption on Ethernet links. A connectivity association (CA) holds a pre-shared key (CAK) and its name (CKN). From that, the switches derive the session keys (SAK) that encrypt the frames. With MKA (802.1X-2010), the switches negotiate and rotate the SAKs. Since 9.3, MKA keychains hold several CAKs with end times for hitless key rollover.

See: `show macsec status [<ports>]`, `macsec connectivity-association <name> connectivity-association-key <cak>`, `macsec mka keychain <name> / key <ckn> cak <cak> endtime <MMddyyyyhhmmss | unlimited>`

## Nickname (spbm nickname, nick-name)

A 2.5-byte short ID of a fabric node (format x.xx.xx, e.g. 1.01.01). It is used to build the multicast MACs for I-SID flooding and must be unique in the fabric. It is set statically or handed out by a dynamic nickname server (Zero Touch Fabric).

See: `spbm 1 nick-name <x.xx.xx>`, `show spbm nick-name`, `spbm nick-name server`

## Routing instance (vrf, virtual router, routing-instances, inet.0)

The Junos VRF. Each instance has its own table (&lt;name&gt;.inet.0); the default table is inet.0. Most show and ping commands take `table <name>.inet.0` or `routing-instance <name>`.

See: `show route <prefix> [exact] [table <instance>.inet.0]`, `ping <ip> source <ip> [routing-instance <ri>] [rapid count <n>] [size <bytes> do-not-fragment]`

## RSMLT (routed smlt)

Layer 3 redundancy for a vIST pair. Each peer also forwards packets sent to the other peer's IP or MAC, so the default gateway keeps working if one peer fails, without VRRP timers.

See: `show ip rsmlt [local | peer] [vrf <vrf>]`, `ip rsmlt [holdup-timer <0-9999>]`

## Segmented VRF (vrf segmentation, trusted, unrestricted, untrusted)

New in 9.4. One VRF is split into three trust segments. Untrusted VLANs (e.g. IoT) can only reach the unrestricted segment (typically the firewall). Trusted VLANs reach trusted and unrestricted. Each segment gets its own L3 VSN I-SID. It needs a Premier or subscription license with an L3 VSN.

See: `segmented`, `vrf <vrf> [trusted | unrestricted | untrusted]`

## SLPP (simple loop prevention protocol, loop protection, slpp guard)

Extreme's loop detection. The switch sends SLPP packets per VLAN; a port that receives its own packets back (above the threshold) is shut down. SLPP Guard on edge ports shuts the port when SLPP packets from another switch arrive. Because the fabric core has no spanning tree, SLPP and BPDU Guard are the main protection against loops built at the access layer.

See: `slpp enable`, `show slpp interface gigabitEthernet [<ports>]`, `slpp-guard enable [timeout <0 | 10-65535>]`

## SPB / SPBM (shortest path bridging, fabric connect, 802.1aq, mac-in-mac, 802.1ah)

Shortest Path Bridging MAC (IEEE 802.1aq) is the technology behind Extreme Fabric Connect. Client frames are wrapped at the edge into a new Ethernet header (MAC-in-MAC, 802.1ah) with backbone MACs and an I-SID. IS-IS calculates loop-free shortest paths between all nodes, so there is no spanning tree in the core. Services (L2 VSN, L3 VSN, multicast) are configured only on the edge switches, not hop by hop.

See: `show isis spbm`, `show isis adjacencies [verbose]`, `show isis spbm nick-name [home | remote]`

## SRX flow mode (flow-based, packet-based, stateful, sessions, security zones)

By default an SRX processes traffic flow-based (stateful). Even when it "only routes", every packet between interfaces needs a session, and that needs a security policy between the zones of the interfaces. If routing looks correct but traffic is dropped, check the zones, policies and sessions before you suspect the routing.

See: `show security flow status`, `show security flow session destination-prefix <ip> [summary]`, `show security policies hit-count`

## System ID (isis system-id, sysid, b-mac, nodal mac)

The 6-byte IS-IS identity of a switch (xxxx.xxxx.xxxx). It is also used as the node's B-MAC in the fabric. Must be unique. You can only change it while IS-IS is disabled. vIST peers reference each other by system ID (smlt-peer-system-id).

See: `show isis system-id`, `system-id <xxxx.xxxx.xxxx>`

## UNI / NNI (user network interface, network network interface, access port, fabric port)

An NNI is a fabric link between two SPB switches (IS-IS adjacency, MAC-in-MAC). A UNI is where clients or legacy devices connect. UNI types are C-VLAN UNI (VLAN mapped to an I-SID), Switched UNI or Flex UNI (port + VLAN tag mapped to an I-SID, no platform VLAN) and Transparent UNI (the whole port, all tags, into one I-SID).

See: `isis / isis spbm 1 / isis enable`, `i-sid <isid> elan`, `i-sid <isid> elan-transparent`

## vIST / SMLT (virtual ist, split multilink trunking, split-beb, virtual bmac, cluster)

Two switches form a cluster for dual-homing. A downstream device connects one LAG to both (SMLT) and sees them as one partner. The vIST is the peer link, carried virtually through the fabric over a VLAN with its own unique I-SID. Toward the fabric, the pair advertises a shared virtual B-MAC; the switch with the lower system ID is the primary split-BEB. Requirements are smlt-peer-system-id, virtual-ist peer-ip, the same MLT IDs, and the same VLAN/I-SID set on both peers.

See: `show virtual-ist`, `show smlt mlt`, `virtual-ist peer-ip <peer-ip> vlan <vist-vlan>`, `spbm 1 smlt-peer-system-id <peer-system-id>`

## Zero Touch Fabric (ztf, zero touch deployment, ztd, onboarding, onboarding i-sid)

A new switch out of the box comes up in Zero Touch mode with all ports in Auto-sense. It forms NNIs on its own, gets a nickname from the nickname server and reaches management (ExtremeCloud IQ / Site Engine) through the onboarding I-SID (default 15999999), where it gets its final config.

See: `spbm nick-name server`, `show spbm nick-name`, `auto-sense onboarding i-sid <isid>`
